comparison: he_full vs he_partial — CKKS encryption coverage ablation
data_provenance: AUTHORITATIVE — built from exact figures in he_full_manifest.json and he_partial_manifest.json, which were themselves rebuilt directly from the real client_*_results.json and server_timing.json files (not console-log transcription).

IMPORTANT_CAVEAT.does_not_match_main_experiment: main.py's Krum/DP-SGD robustness experiments use 38 features (full ~736,046-row corpus). This ablation used 35, because build_partitions.py was run with --max-rows 100000, which subsamples the corpus before VarianceThreshold is fit. Confirmed directly via the num_features:35 field present in every client config in both conditions' authoritative result JSON.
IMPORTANT_CAVEAT.impact_on_this_comparison: internally valid — both conditions share identical partition files, so the full-vs-partial comparison below isolates HE_FULL_COVERAGE cleanly. Only becomes a problem if these numbers are compared directly against main.py's 38-feature results without noting the difference.
IMPORTANT_CAVEAT.recommended_action: rebuild via 'python build_partitions.py --model-type network --num-clients 2' (no --max-rows) before finalizing any cross-experiment table. Not yet done.

client_side_he_encrypt_latency_s.finding: Partial HE is ~17-19x faster than full-coverage HE at client-side encryption, tracking closely with the 27.65x ratio in encrypted parameter count (129,352 / 4,680). The sub-linear speedup relative to the param-count ratio reflects fixed per-chunk overhead in CKKS chunking that doesn't scale down proportionally for very small payloads (partial HE still needed 3 chunks vs full HE's 64, not a proportionally smaller number).

server_side_aggregation_latency_s.finding: Server-side homomorphic aggregation shows the same directional effect as client-side encryption — partial HE is ~14x faster to aggregate — confirming the cost scales with encrypted-parameter volume on BOTH sides of the protocol, not just client-side encryption. This wasn't fully visible in the console transcript and is a new figure only available from the authoritative server_timing.json files.

peak_ram_comparison_mb.finding: Peak RAM is essentially identical between conditions (within ~1MB, well inside run-to-run noise), contradicting the original ablation design doc's prediction that full-coverage HE would show meaningfully higher peak RAM. The authoritative per-stage data confirms why: in he_full, the HE encryption stage itself peaks at only 68-88MB (stage_peaks.he_encrypt), a small fraction of the training subprocess's 364-374MB peak that dominates the round. In he_partial, HE's stage peak is smaller still (~60-63MB) but the round's overall peak is STILL set by training, not encryption, in both conditions. At this model's small size (~130K params, well under 1MB even fully flattened to float64), HE's memory footprint cannot meaningfully move overall peak RAM regardless of encryption scope.

round_avg_ram_anomaly.finding: he_partial's client_0 round 1 shows round_avg_mb=347.2MB, sharply higher than its own rounds 2-3 (~205-206MB) and than client_1's entire run (~197-201MB throughout). This is confirmed in the authoritative data (not a console-transcription artifact) via the before_round/after_train/after_he snapshots, which all sit near 59-60MB for round 1 — meaning the elevated round_avg comes from the round_avg_mb aggregate calculation over the RamSampler's continuous background polling during training, not from the process's own snapshot readings. Most consistent explanation: a one-time process/OS-level warm-up effect specific to being the very first round sampled in this condition's run (client_0 also shows the same pattern, a slightly elevated first round, in he_full: 202.7MB vs 218-219MB in rounds 2-3 there too — though in he_full round 1 is LOWER not higher, so the direction of the anomaly isn't even consistent between conditions). Recommend treating this as sampling/measurement noise specific to round 1 rather than a real HE-scope-driven effect, and considering exclusion or footnoting of round-1 RAM-average figures in any formal report.

train_time_sanity_check.finding: Rounds 2-3 converge closely across conditions for both clients (~42s and ~42s for client_0; ~29s for client_1 in both), confirming training cost is independent of HE scope as expected — HE happens strictly after training on the already-trained parameters. he_full's client_0 round 1 (48.76s) is a mild outlier versus its own rounds 2-3 and versus he_partial's round 1 (41.98s) for the same client — consistent with a one-time subprocess/JIT warm-up on the very first round of the first condition executed, not a genuine HE-scope-driven training cost.

conclusion_draft_for_paper: At this model scale (~130K parameters, 35 features), restricting CKKS encryption to the classifier head (3.6% of parameters) yields a ~17-19x reduction in client-side encryption latency and a ~14x reduction in server-side aggregation latency compared to full-model encryption, with no measurable difference in peak client-side RAM (within ~1MB across all four client-round combinations) — training memory dominates the round's peak footprint regardless of HE scope. This suggests partial HE's primary benefit at this scale is latency on both the client and server side, not memory pressure; the RAM argument for partial HE becomes relevant only at model sizes where the flattened parameter vector itself begins to rival or exceed training memory, which this ~130K-parameter model does not reach. Note: this result was obtained on a 35-feature model (100k-row subsampled partitions); the main experiment's 38-feature full-corpus model has not yet been tested under this ablation and the comparison should be re-run before final publication to confirm the finding holds at the correct feature count.
